messages.author: 55d1a09c85eadab7
messages.subject: Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
parts:
Hi,

I tried 3 simple varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal (attached files).

Q1. I believe that those 3 models are equivalent (apart from reparameterization). Is that correct?

But, the result of model1 doesn't converge at all. Scaling data doesn't matter.

Q2. Could you tell me the reason?

# I'm using Stan 2.9.0-3 and R-3.2.5 on Windows 7.

Regards,
Bee

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
parts:
Those aren't the same models (at least not without
the appropriate Jacobian adjustments), because
of the change of variables.

model1: uniform on 2 x 2 covariance matrics

model2: independent uniform on correlation and scales

The map between the two isn't linear, so you need a Jacobian
to make them the same model.

Centering as well as scaling X would probably help with
fitting a and b, as would weakly informative priors on
all the parameters.

- Bob

It's doing an elementwise multiplication by X.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
parts:
That's not uniform and violates the basic Stan principle
that all legal values for parameters should have support
(not all the legal parameter values here produce positive
definite matrices).

If you really want uniform over covariance matrices, it has
to be this:

parameters {
cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
...

Of course, that's improper, so you need to make sure you
have some data so the posterior's proper.

But we recommend scaling a Cholesky factor of a correlation
matrix with some prior concentration around the unit correlation
matrix.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
parts:
You don't need a sampling statement. For every parameter
type Stan has, the default distribution is uniform over
values satisfying the constraint. In this case, the
uniform happens to be improper.

If you want to know how we represent it as unconstrained
parameters, transform, and calculate the Jacobian, there's
a chapter on all the transforms we use near the end of the
manual. The unconstrained representation is a Cholesky factor
with log-transformed diagonals (Cholesky factors with positive
diagonals are a basis for the symmetric, positive-definite
matrices). The Jacobian's in the chapter, and it gets applied
automatically behind the scenes (and differentiated) for
each leapfrog step.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
parts:
On Monday, April 18, 2016 at 2:29:31 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
You don't need a sampling statement.  For every parameter
type Stan has, the default distribution is uniform over
values satisfying the constraint.  In this case, the
uniform happens to be improper.

A bit more background on this in case it's helpful: Stan works by starting with a log probability variable (lp__) initialized to zero and then adding to it when a sampling statement or increment_log_prob() is used. Therefore if you declare a parameter and then don't give it a prior nothing will be added to the log probability and you get a uniform prior by default. Anyway, just wanted to make clear that it's not that Stan sneaks in a call to uniform() under the hood if you don't specify a prior or anything like that.

Jonah

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
parts:
What Stan sneaks in under the hood is the Jacobian
of any constraints. All of our underlying calculations in
sampling are after we unconstrain parameters.

So if you write

parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;

Then we log-transform to unconstrained scale and sample over log(sigma).
But then we need to exp()-transform back and add the Jacobian to get
a uniform distribution for sigma over (0, infinity).

So it works out to the same thing (including what the lp__ value
is going to be) as

parameters {
real sigma_raw;
...
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
sigma <- exp(sigma_raw);
...
model {
// Jacobian adjustment, log(abs(d/d.u exp(u))) = log(exp(u)) = u
increment_log_prob(sigma);

Now sigma has an improper uniform distribution over (0, infinity)
and sigma_raw is the log transform of sigma. And it's not just
virtually identical, it's really identical down to the operations
being run in the generated C++ code.

- Bob
